name: Dihexa

lead: Dihexa is a lab-made peptide derived from angiotensin IV, designed to resist breakdown and cross the blood-brain barrier. Nootropic users take it for memory and learning, which they tie to study and work performance rather than to looks.

It is reported to bind hepatocyte growth factor and boost signalling through the c-Met receptor, promoting synapse formation in cell cultures. It has been studied in rodents for memory impairment, and a 2021 study reported it rescued cognitive impairment in an Alzheimer mouse model, linked to the PI3K/AKT pathway. No human trial has been published.

paras: It is sold as a research chemical and discussed in nootropic communities. There is no established human routine.
Human safety is unknown. Authors have raised the theoretical concern that sustained c-Met activation could promote tumors. It is not an approved drug.

angle.text: Dihexa is taken by nootropic users for sharper memory and focus, which they connect to study and work performance. It has been studied in rodents for memory, and no human trials exist.

lead: Dihexa is a synthetic oligopeptide analog of angiotensin IV, modified to be more stable and to penetrate the brain [1][2]. It emerged from work on angiotensin IV analogs as potential antidementia agents [2][3].

Preclinical studies report that angiotensin IV-derived peptides act through the hepatocyte growth factor/c-Met system [4], and a 2021 study reported that dihexa rescued cognitive impairment in the APP/PS1 Alzheimer mouse model [5]. No human clinical trials have been published.

paras: Reviewers describe the HGF/c-Met system as a target for Alzheimer disease treatment [6]. Research indicates that procognitive and synaptogenic effects of angiotensin IV-derived peptides depend on activating this system [4]. Grokipedia reports high-affinity binding to hepatocyte growth factor and a long half-life in rats [1].
No studies found. Related research is preclinical: a mouse Alzheimer model study reported improved memory and activation of PI3K/AKT signalling [5].
It is sold as a research chemical and discussed among nootropic users. No community sources are cited here.
